result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_kirchhoff_index()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the Kirchhoff index (total resistance) of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L49974-L50083){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Kirchhoff index](/assets/graphs/get-kirchhoff-index.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph labeled with the resistance distance across each edge: 1 on the two tail edges, but 0.75 on the four cycle edges (accent), where a second route runs in parallel. Summing resistance over all 15 pairs gives the Kirchhoff index 21.0." width="100%"} The Kirchhoff index is the sum of all pairwise resistance distances: `Kf(G) = Σᵢ<ⱼ Ω(i,j)` It can also be computed from the Laplacian eigenvalues: `Kf(G) = n × Σₖ (1/λₖ)` where `λₖ` are the non-zero eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix. This method uses the eigenvalue form, which needs a single eigendecomposition. The Kirchhoff index is a single-number summary of how well-connected a whole network is, treating every edge as a 1-ohm resistor (see `get_resistance_distance()`). Lower values mean the nodes are, on the whole, joined by more numerous and shorter routes. It is used to: - compare the overall robustness of different network designs with the same number of nodes - characterize molecular graphs in chemistry (it was introduced as a molecular descriptor) - measure how adding or removing an edge changes global connectivity Edge weights are ignored, parallel edges act as resistors in parallel, and self-loops are ignored. The value grows with the number of nodes, so compare graphs of similar size, or divide by the number of node pairs for an average resistance. The computation is a dense `O(n^3)` eigendecomposition, which becomes slow for graphs with many thousands of nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Kirchhoff index. Returns `0.0` for graphs with fewer than two nodes, and infinity (`inf`) for disconnected graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Kirchhoff index $Kf(G) = \sum_{i < j} \Omega(i, j)$ (Klein and Randić, 1993) is the electrical analogue of the Wiener index, using effective resistance in place of shortest-path distance. A striking spectral identity ties it to the Laplacian directly: $Kf(G) = n \sum_{k \ge 2} \tfrac{1}{\lambda_k}$, summing reciprocals of the non-zero Laplacian eigenvalues, which makes small $\lambda_2$ (poor expansion) inflate $Kf$ and sharp expander graphs bring it down. Complete graphs saturate the lower bound $Kf \ge n - 1$; disconnected graphs give $+\infty$ because some resistances diverge (detected as more than one zero eigenvalue). Cost is $O(n^3)$ via full Laplacian eigendecomposition, and only undirected inputs make sense because the electrical analogue requires reversibility. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path graph's Kirchhoff index grows with roughly the cube of its size, since resistance distances accumulate over many series connections. For 4 nodes the pairwise resistances are 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, and 3, which sum to 10: ::: {#3310f3c1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(4) # Returns about 10.0 path.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9.999999999999998 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph is the most efficiently connected case, so its Kirchhoff index is as low as possible: exactly `n - 1`: ::: {#8e8d3335 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} complete = ec.Graph() complete.add_full_graph(4) # Returns 3.0 complete.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3.0 ``` ::: ::: Adding an edge can only lower the index. Closing the 4-node path into a cycle gives every pair a second route and drops the index from 10 to 5: ::: {#094d8f75 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(4) cycle.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 5.0 ``` ::: ::: A disconnected graph has infinite resistance between components that can't reach each other, so the Kirchhoff index diverges: ::: {#bf3211c6 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") # No edge between A and B # Returns inf g.get_kirchhoff_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` inf ``` ::: :::
